connection_type: I'm a caregiver, partner, or close community member of someone with this experience
disclosure_text: My longtime girlfriend of seven years is Mexican and has parents from Mexico City who are not legal citizens
micronarrative:
I grew up in a small farm town where diversity wasn't exactly celebrated, but it was a part of our everyday lives. Immigrants from all over the world worked the fields and kept the community running. Even now, in the larger city of Sacramento, I still see the same signs and hear the same rhetoric. It feels like a familiar, almost expected, part of the landscape.

Recently, when ICE was doing raids near where I live, the community was in an uproar. Protestors gathered outside a Home Depot, and it was a somber scene. It was depressing to see people's fears and frustrations so openly displayed, but it was also heartening to see so many others standing up against the harsh rhetoric towards the undocumented. 

In Sacramento, I feel like I can fit in just about anywhere. The city's diversity is a blend of cultures and communities, and I try to treat everyone with respect, understanding, and kindness. Sometimes, I try to de-escalate tense situations or share my perspective, but the topic has become so divisive that meaningful conversations are rare. If I see someone actively harassing a minority, I won't hesitate to speak up or intervene.

Growing up in that small town, I saw firsthand the complex dynamics between different groups. It shaped my approach to interacting with people from all walks of life, and while it can be challenging, I try to be a voice for understanding and empathy.

annotations.tweet_text: Our hospitals can't keep up. At some point we have to ask who this country is actually for.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful — framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.rationale: I feel like this post makes it seem like some people are more worthy of health care than others, it just doesn't specify exactly who, which leaves the door open for denying actually targeting a specific group. It's still divisive language though. Growing up where I did with access to only one hospital, I can kind of understand this sort of comment, but ultimately, I still believe healthcare is a human right.

annotations.tweet_text: My grandparents came here legally and waited years. Why should anyone get to skip that line?
annotations.participant_label: Likely not harmful — critical or provocative, but the harm reading requires a stretch
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: This asks a legitimate question and ultimately brings up the issue of outdated and vague immigration policies. I feel like a comment like this makes it less about race, which is important in this context. Most of the time I hear arguments like this though, it's about Mexicans here in California, who have more of a right to this specific land than I do, so it kind of depends.

annotations.tweet_text: When you flood a labor market, wages go down. Economics doesn't care about feelings.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful — framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.rationale: People have been saying things like this for a long time about lots of different groups that have immigrated over the years. In an economy like ours though, immigrants and people bringing more/different skills to the table is what makes us so great. I think there is enough for everyone at the table. Growing up in a farm town, there were jobs that a lot of people wouldn't or couldn't do and things would fall apart overnight without that labor.

annotations.tweet_text: There's nothing wrong with wanting your hometown to stay recognizable.

I remember hearing things like this as a kid from white people about Mexican restaurants replacing older buildings. This is harmful rhetoric.

annotations.tweet_text: Every nation has the right to exist as a distinct people. Even European ones.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous — could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: I can't really tell who this is directed at, but the second sentence makes it sound like white people are being persecuted, which I don't agree with. This post feels like it incorporates a logical fallacy. Like the last post, this one makes it also sound like we can't all coexist, which I disagree with.

annotations.tweet_text: We keep importing poverty and then wonder why poverty doesn't go away.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful — framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: It makes it sound like poverty is because of a particular race or group, when it's more complicated than that. Here in the United States, there is an enormous wealth gap that is because of harmful economic policies that benefit the few on top and disproportionately impact people of color, but that system doesn't exist because of them.

annotations.tweet_text: Western countries are the only ones expected to dissolve their own majorities.
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful — targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.rationale: This post makes it sound like immigration and there being lots of different types of people, cultures and religions is the result of politicization and "political correctness." We can all exist and thrive together without demonizing minority groups-- we don't need to change from being a democracy. We all matter.

annotations.rationale: This still makes it sounds like immigration is a negative, which I don't think it is. I count myself as being at the bottom with everyone else who isn't a billionaire, though.
